'''what<sup>1</sup>''' (hwot), ''pron.''   [< ME. ''wh'' ''quat, qwat, hwat, hwet'' (gen. ''w'' ''wham, whom,'' acc. ''what, whet''), < ''hwæs,'' dat. ''hwam, hwæm,'' acc. ''hwa'' ''huat'' = OFries. ''hwet'' = D. ''wat'' = M OHG. ''hwaz, waz,'' MHG. ''waz,'' G. ''w'' = Dan. Sw. ''hvad'' = Goth. ''hwa'' rogative and indefinite, also inte L. ''quid,'' what (indefinite), somewh = Skt. ''kat;'' neut. of the pron. ''Whose'' is historically the gen. of than of ''who;'' and it is still so us equivalent to ''of which''), although ties object, and it is becoming '''A.''' ''interrog.'' '''1.''' Used absolutely gative pronoun. {{smaller|(''a'') Applied to inan}}
{{smaller block|Quat hast thu don . . . sin Saterdai {{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), iii. 196.}}}}
{{smaller block|Shame then it was that drove him from the Parlament, but the shame of ''what?'' {{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, vi.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Folks at her House at such an Hour!
Lord! ''what'' will all the Neighbours say?</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', The Dove, st. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|I believe they are in actual consultation upon ''what'''s for supper. {{right|''Goldsmith'', She Stoops to Conquer, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|''What'' can restrain the agony of a mother’s heart? {{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 40.}}}}
(''b'') Applied to animals (and sometimes in contempt to persons) with the force of inquiry after the nature or kind: as, ''what'' is that running up the tree? (''c'') Applied to persons: nearly equivalent to ''who'', but having reference to origin or character, rather than to name or identity.
{{smaller block|<poem>“''What'' is this womman,” quod I, “so worthily atired?”
“That is Mede the mayde,” quod she.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), ii. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thise tweyne come to the messagers, and hem asked ''what'' thei were, and thei ansuerde that thei sholde sone knowe, yef it plesed hem to a-byde. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 129.}}}}
{{smaller block|''What'''s he that walks alone so sadly, with his hands behind him? {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Woman-Hater, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Eminent titles may, indeed, inform who their owners are, not often ''what''. {{right|''Ford'', Perkin Warbeck, Ded.}}}}
(''d'') Used in various elliptical and incomplete constructions: as, ''what?'' equivalent to ''what did you say?'' or ''what is it?'' (''e'') Used in exclamation, to express surprise, indignation, etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Hwat!'' wulle ȝe this pes to-breke,
And do than kinge swuche schame?</poem>
{{right|''Owl and Nightingale'', l. 1730 (Morris and Skeat, I. 191).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>“''What!''” quod the prest to Perkyn, “Peter! as me thinketh,
Thow art lettred a litel; who lerned the on boke?”</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), vii. 130.}}}}

{{smaller block|But ''what'', shall the abuse of a thing make the right vse odious?
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie (ed. Arber), p. 54.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''What!'' are the ladies of your land so tall?</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, ii.}}}}
{{smaller|(''f'') Expressing a summons.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''La. Cap.'' Nurse, where’s my daughter? call her forth to me.
''Nurse.'' . . . I bade her come. ''What'', lamb! ''what'', lady-bird!
God forbid! Where’s this girl? ''What'', Juliet?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., i. 3. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Qua.'' [Within.] ''What'', Simplicius!
''Sim.'' I come, Quadratus. ''Marston'', What you Will, v. 1.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|Chamberlain, call in the music, bid the tapsters and maids come up and dance; ''what!'' we’ll make a night of it.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|(''g''†) A general introductory notion, equivalent to ‘well,’ ‘lo,’ ‘now,’ etc., and constituting a mere expletive.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''What'', welcome be the cut, a Goddes name!</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 854.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''What'', will you walk with me about the town?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., i. 2. 22.}}}}
'''2.''' Used adjectively and lending an interrogative force to the proposition in which it occurs. {{smaller|(''a'') Inquiring as to the individual being, character, kind, or sort of a definite thing or person.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Allas! ''what'' womman wil ye of me make?</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 1305.}}}}
{{smaller block|''What'' manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?
{{right|Mark iv. 41.}}}}
{{smaller block|''What'' news on the Rialto?
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 3. 39.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''What'' good should follow this, if this were done?
''What'' harm, undone? ''Tennyson'', Passing of Arthur.</poem>}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Inquiring as to extent or quantity: equivalent to the question ''how much?''}}
{{smaller block|“''What'' money have you got, Copperfield?” he said. . . . I told him seven shillings. {{right|''Dickens'', David Copperfield, vi.}}}}

(''c'') Used intensively or emphatically with a force varying from the interrogative to the exclamatory: often followed by the indefinite article: as, ''what'' an idea!

{{smaller block|''What'' manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness?
{{right|2 Pet. iii. 11.}}}}

{{smaller block|''What'' a piece of work is a man! how noble in reason! how infinite in faculty! {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, ii. 2. 315.}}}}

{{smaller block|''What'' confusion and mischeif do the avarice, anger, and ambition of Princes cause in the world!
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, March 24, 1672.}}}}

<poem>Oh, Amos Cottle!—Phœbus! ''what'' a name,
To fill the speaking trump of future fame!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Byron'', English Bards and Scotch Reviewers.}}}}

<poem>Oh, ''what'' a dawn of day!
How the March sun feels like May!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Browning'', A Lover’s Quarrel.}}}}

'''What an (and) if†?''' Same as ''what if?''

<poem>And ''what an if''
His sorrows have so overwhelm’d his wits,
Shall we be thus afflicted in his wreaks?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iv. 4. 9.}}}}

'''What else?''' what else can or could be the case: an elliptical expression expecting no answer, and hence sometimes equivalent to a strong affirmation.

<poem>''Licio.'' But cans’t thou blow it?
''Huntsman. What else?''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Lyly'', Midas, iv. 3.}}}}

'''What . . . for? what for?''' what . . . as? what kind of? in such phrases as, ''what for'' a man is he?—that is, what kind of man, in looks or character? It is equivalent to the German idiom ''was für ein'', and as reflecting that idiom is used in the English of the Pennsylvania Germans and their The earlier idiom ''what'' . . . ''for'' is now rare.

{{smaller block|''What'' ’s he ''for'' a man?
{{right|''Peele'', Edward I. (ed. Dyce), p. 383.}}}}
{{smaller block|''What'' is he ''for'' a fool that betroths himself to unquietness?
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, i. 3. 49.}}}}

'''What ho !''' an exclamatory summons or call.

<poem>''Gads. What, ho !'' chamberlain!
''Cham.'' [Within.] At hand, quoth pick-purse.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 1. 52.}}}}

'''What if?''' elliptical for ''what would happen if? what would you say if? what matters it if?'' etc.

<poem>''What if'' this mixture do not work at all? . . .
''What if'' it be a poison?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iv. 3. 21.}}}}
<poem>''What if'' he dwells on many a fact as though
Some things Heaven knew not which it ought to know? . . .
Such are the prayers his people love to hear.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', A Family Record.}}}}

'''What is thee ?'''† what is the matter with thee?

<poem>Lefdy, ''what is the?'' . . .
Me were leffre to beo ded
Thane iseo the make such chere.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 50.}}}}

'''What not''', elliptical for ''what may I not say?'' implying ‘everything else; various other things; et cetera; what you will’: as, the table was loaded with toys, pictures, and ''what not.'' Hence ''what-not, n.''

{{smaller block|Such air is unwholesome, and engenders melancholy, plagues, and ''what not.''
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 150.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thou art like to meet with, in the way which thou goest, . . . lions, dragons, darkness, and, in a word, death, and ''what not.''
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|College A cannot compete with College B unless it has more scholarships, unless it changes the time of election to scholarships, or ''what not.''
{{right|''Contemporary Rev.'', LI. 617.}}}}

'''What of?''' (''a'') Elliptical for ''what comes of?''—that is, what care you (I, we, etc.)? does it matter in any way?

{{smaller block|All this is so; but ''what of'' this, my lord?
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, iv. 1. 73.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Elliptical for ''what say or think you of?''}}
{{smaller block|To-day? but ''what of'' yesterday?
{{right|''Tennyson'', The Ancient Sage.}}}}

{{smaller|'''What’s his (its) name? what do you call it?''' etc., colloquial phrases generally signifying that the speaker cannot supply a definite name for some person or thing, either because the name has escaped his memory, or because the person or thing is of so trivial consequence that he or it is not deserving of a specific name. The phrases are sometimes formed into a compound: as, tell Mr. ''What’s-his-name'' to be off. See ''what-d’ye-call-it.''}}
{{smaller block|Good even, good Master ''What-ye-call’t.''
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iii. 3. 74.}}}}
{{smaller|'''What’s to do here?''' See ''do''<sup>1</sup>.—'''What though?''' See ''though.''}}

'''B.''' ''rel.'' '''1.''' A compound relative pronoun, meaning ‘that which,’ or having a value including the simple relative pronoun ''which'' with the demonstrative pronoun ''that'' preceding: as, “''what'' I have written I have written” (that is, ''that which'' I have written I have written). It is no longer used of persons, except in the anomalous phrase ''but what.''
{{smaller block|Mekli than to Meliors he munged [told] ''what'' he thougt.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2578.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Loke up, I seye, and telle me ''what'' she is
Anon, that I may gon aboute thy nede.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 862.}}}}
{{smaller block|I am ''what'' I was born to be, your prince.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, v. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|A host of second-rate critics, and official critics, and ''what'' is called “the popular mind” as well.
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Literature and Dogma, vi. 5.}}}}

{{smaller block|''What'', as strictly equivalent to the relative which, never had much vogue, and has long been a vulgarism; but its genitive [whose] has survived, in preference to whichs, as we should have modernized the medieval quhilkes.
{{right|''F. Hall'', False Philology, p. 7, note.}}}}

{{smaller|''What'' was formerly and in vulgar speech is still used as a simple relative, equivalent to ''that'' or ''which'': as, if I had a donkey ''what'' wouldn’t go.}}
{{smaller block|Offer them peace or aught ''what'' is beside.
{{right|''Peele'', Edward I. (Old Plays, II. 37).}}}}
{{smaller block|The matter ''what'' other men wrote.
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 142.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I fear nothing
''What'' can be said against me.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., v. 1. 126.}}}}

{{smaller|''What'' has also the value of ''whatever'' or ''whoever'': as, come ''what'' will, I shall be there.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''What'' in the world he is
That names me traitor, villain-like he lies.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, v. 3. 97.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Let come ''what'' come may, . . .
I shall have had my day.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, xi.}}}}

'''2.''' Used adjectively, meaning ‘that . . . which,’ or having compound relative value: as, I know ''what'' book you mean (that is, I know ''that'' book ''which'' you mean); he makes the most of ''what'' money he has (that is, he makes the most of ''that'' money ''which'' he has): applied to persons and things. {{smaller|(''a'') That . . . who or which; those . . . who or which.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Shal nat be told for me . . .
. . . ''what'' jeweles men in the fyr tho caste.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 2087.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
